To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Na(+)-inflow by Na(+)/Ca(2+)--exchange is about twice as high as Na(+)-inflows via light-activated channels.
Na(+)- and K(+)-currents through voltage-dependent channels and the Ca(2+)/Na(+) exchange current contribute substantially to the photoreceptor's response to light.
Na(+) and Ca(2+) influx and Na(+)/Ca(2+ )-exchange activity are quantitatively determined in blowfly Callipora photoreceptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the quantitative analysis of Ca(2+), Na(+), and H(+) fluxes and their role in the regulation of the membrane potential in blowfly photoreceptors.
the biophysics of the light-induced changes of the membrane potential in the photoreceptors of the blowfly Calliphoravicia.
the biophysics and biochemistry of visual transduction in the blowfly Calliphor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na(+)/Ca(2+)+exchange is an effective mechanism for Na(+)-regulating the light-activated Ca(2+)+-influx.
the Na(+)/Ca(2+), K(+) and Cl(-) homeostasis in photoreceptors is achieved by Na(+)/K(+)-pumps, Na(+)-channels and Na+/Ca(+)-exchangers.
the Na+/Ca( 2+) -exchanger is a very important component of the Na(+) homeostasis in photoreceptors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca(2+), Na(+), and K(+) are regulated through the activity of light-activated channels and Na+/Ca(+)-exchange, while Na(+) and K(+) also are regulated by Na(+)/K(+)-pump activity.
the Na+/Ca( 2+) -exchanger plays a major role in the control of intracellular Na+ concentration, and that the Na(+)/K(+)-pump is the major Na(+)-extruding mechanism.
the Ca(2+), Na(+)-inflow and Na(+)/Ca(2+), K(+)-exchange are all involved in the phototransduction process of blowfly photoreceptors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Na+/Ca( 2+)-exchange in blowfly photoreceptors is a very efficient mechanism to regulate intracellular Na(+) concentration.
the Ca(2+), Na(+), and K+ concentrations are tightly coupled in the photoreceptor.
the Na+/Ca( 2+) -exchanger is the dominant mechanism of Na(+) -influx in the dark-adapted photoreceptor and the Na(+) -channel the dominant mechanism of influx in the light-adapted state.
